scenario: AITA for refusing to loan my brother my vacation money? | My (21F) brother (30M) and I live with our parents. He’s in a shitty job trying to get out so he went back to school and that’s why he moved back in 1 1/2 years ago. I’m in third year university and working to put myself through. I’m in business school which I am finding to difficult but not impossible. I should graduate in 2 years. When I got into uni I started saving for a bit of all my paycheques (whatever I could manage; sometimes it was as much as 15% and others as low as 1%) to go on a big vacation post uni gradation. Probably a cruise, Japan or a trip to different countries in Europe I’ve never been to. It has about $2800 in it now. My brother has not been on a vacation in many years and keeps hinting that he needs one. My parents already help him financially so he wouldn’t ask them for more help for that. Last week when he was complaining to my parents about it, they mentioned me and my vacation fund and said he could’ve been doing that all these years to be able to afford to go somewhere, or he could start now and maybe be able to go across country in a year. 3 days ago he came to me and asked if he could borrow my vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or Fall. He said since I won’t need it for another 2 years it’s plenty of time for him to pay me back. I said no. My brother is horrible with money. He makes about as much as I do yet always seems to be broke despite never buying groceries or paying rent (for the record, I do not pay rent either, which is why I have been able to build up the fund, but I do buy most of my own groceries, as well as pay for all my makeup, health supplies, phone and uni fees). He’s very mad I said no. He says it’s jor fair as the youngest child I got to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it’s not fair I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went whereas he had to go back. He says I’ve only been able to save so much money because “mom and dad spoiled me.” I disagree. My father, as well as my uni accounting and finance classes taught me to budget. If anything I think my parents spoiled him Because doesn’t know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he will be able to pay me back in time. Even if he couldn’t roger he could... I’m uncomfortable. AITA?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm being unfair to my brother by refusing to lend him my vacation money. Let me start by laying out the situation as I understand it. First, I'm 21, and my brother is 30. We both live with our parents. My brother is in a tough job and went back to school, which is why he moved back in. I'm in my third year of university, working to put myself through business school, which I find challenging but manageable. I plan to graduate in two years. When I started university, I began saving a portion of my paychecks, sometimes as much as 15% and other times as low as 1%, to go on a big vacation after graduation. My goal is to take a cruise, visit Japan, or travel through Europe. Right now, my vacation fund has about $2,800. My brother hasn't been on a vacation in many years and keeps hinting that he needs one. My parents already help him financially, so he wouldn't ask them for more help. Last week, when he was complaining to my parents about needing a vacation, they mentioned my vacation fund and suggested he could start saving now to maybe go somewhere in a year. Three days ago, he came to me and asked if he could borrow my vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or fall. He said since I won't need it for another two years, there's plenty of time for him to pay me back. I said no. My brother is horrible with money. He makes about the same as I do, but he's always broke despite never buying groceries or paying rent (I don't pay rent either, which is why I've been able to build up the fund). I buy most of my groceries, makeup, health supplies, phone, and uni fees. He's very mad that I said no. He says it's not fair because, as the youngest child, I get to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it's not fair that I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went, whereas he had to go back. He also says I've only been able to save so much money because mom and dad spoiled me. I disagree. My father, as well as my university accounting and finance classes, taught me to budget. I think my parents spoiled him because he doesn't know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his job. I don't think it's fair for me to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he'll be able to pay me back in time, even if he could. I'm feeling uncomfortable about this situation. Is it fair for me to refuse to lend him the money? Am I being unreasonable? Okay, so to break this down, I need to consider several factors: financial responsibility, fairness, family dynamics, and future implications. First, financial responsibility. I have a clear goal for my savings, which is my post-graduation vacation. I've been consistent in saving, even if the percentage varies. My brother, on the other hand, has a history of being bad with money. He's always broke despite not having certain expenses like rent or groceries. This makes me question his ability to repay the loan, especially since he's already in a tough financial situation. Second, fairness. My brother feels it's unfair that I get to go on a vacation while he doesn't. He's older and had to move out earlier, which might have limited his opportunities. However, I started saving specifically for this purpose, and it's a goal I've been working towards. He's also receiving financial help from our parents, which I'm not. He's suggesting that I'm being spoiled, but I see my savings as a result of budgeting and financial education, not spoiling. Third, family dynamics. My parents mentioned my vacation fund when he was complaining, which might have given him the idea to ask me. However, I have to consider my own goals and financial stability. My brother's anger seems to stem from feeling neglected or less supported compared to me. This could be a deeper issue in our family dynamics, but I'm not sure how to address that right now. Fourth, future implications. If I lend him the money and he doesn't repay it, it could strain our relationship further. It might also affect my ability to go on my planned vacation, which is something I've been looking forward to. On the other hand, if I refuse, he might continue to be angry, which could create a tense living situation. I also need to think about alternatives. Maybe instead of borrowing the entire amount, he could contribute to the fund or find another way to save. But given his track record, I'm skeptical he'd be able to do that consistently. Another angle is the concept of fairness within the family. My brother feels that I'm getting more support, but I see my savings as a result of my own efforts. It's possible that our parents have different ways of supporting us, which might contribute to his feelings of unfairness. I also wonder if there's a way to compromise. Maybe I could lend him a smaller amount or set strict terms for repayment. However, given his history of poor money management, I'm not sure if that's a viable option. In terms of fairness, I believe I'm entitled to keep my savings for my own goals. My brother's situation is difficult, but I've been responsible with my money, and I shouldn't have to sacrifice my plans to help him, especially when he's already receiving financial support from our parents. I also think about the principle of not lending money to people who can't repay it. It's a common financial advice to avoid lending money to friends or family if there's a risk they won't be able to pay it back. In this case, my brother's history suggests he might not be able to repay the loan, making it a risky proposition. Additionally, I should consider the emotional impact. If I lend him the money and he doesn't repay it, it could lead to resentment and further strain our relationship. On the other hand, refusing might make him angry, but it's better to maintain my financial independence and goals. I also need to reflect on why my brother is so upset. Is it because he feels he's not getting the same opportunities as me, or is it because he's struggling financially and sees my savings as an easy solution? Understanding his perspective might help, but I also have to stand firm on my own needs and goals. In conclusion, while I understand my brother's frustration and financial struggles, I believe it's reasonable to refuse the loan. My savings are for a specific goal, and my brother's history of poor money management makes it unlikely he'll be able to repay the loan in time. Additionally, I've been responsible with my money, and it's fair that I keep it for my own plans.
